questions.stem: Which is one of the Australian Government's economic objectives?
options: Zero unemployment
Price stability
A fixed exchange rate
A balanced budget every year
questions.explanation: The objectives include higher quality of life, economic growth, full employment, price stability, equitable distribution of income and wealth, and environmental sustainability. Full employment allows some frictional and structural unemployment, so it is not zero unemployment.

questions.stem: Strong economic growth raises employment but also adds to greenhouse gas emissions. This is an example of:
options: a complementary pair of economic objectives
a policy lag in environmental policy
a market-based environmental instrument
a conflict between economic objectives
questions.explanation: Pursuing one objective, growth, can work against another, environmental sustainability. Such trade-offs constrain the government's ability to achieve all objectives at once.

questions.stem: In the short term, a policy that lowers unemployment by boosting aggregate demand is most likely to conflict with the objective of:
options: economic growth
higher quality of life
full employment
price stability
questions.explanation: As spare capacity is used up, stronger demand puts upward pressure on wages and prices. This short-term trade-off between unemployment and inflation is a key constraint on policy.

questions.stem: A government increases income support payments, funded by higher taxes on high incomes. Some economists argue this could reduce work incentives. This illustrates a possible conflict between:
options: environmental sustainability and price stability
economic growth and a higher quality of life for all
equitable distribution of income and economic growth
price stability and full employment
questions.explanation: Redistribution improves equity, but higher marginal tax rates and payments that are withdrawn as income rises may weaken incentives to work and invest, slowing growth. This is the equity-efficiency trade-off.

questions.stem: Which is an external constraint on the Australian Government achieving its economic objectives?
options: A downturn in the economies of Australia's major trading partners
A decision by the Monetary Policy Board to change the cash rate
A change in the rate of the GST agreed with the state governments
A rise in government spending on infrastructure in regional areas
questions.explanation: Australia is a small open economy, so falling demand abroad lowers exports and growth regardless of domestic policy. The other choices are domestic policy decisions.

questions.stem: Microeconomic policies differ from macroeconomic policies because they:
options: manage the level of aggregate demand to smooth the business cycle over time
are set by the Reserve Bank rather than by the Australian Government
aim only to change the value of the Australian dollar against other major currencies
target particular industries and markets to improve efficiency and productivity
questions.explanation: Microeconomic policy works on the supply side, improving how resources are used in particular markets. Fiscal and monetary policy are the main macroeconomic, demand-side tools.

questions.stem: National Competition Policy, introduced in the mid-1990s, aimed mainly to:
options: reduce the number of firms in each industry to achieve economies of scale
set the prices of essential goods and services across all of the states
increase competition in markets such as energy, transport and utilities
protect local manufacturers from imports by raising tariff rates
questions.explanation: Following the Hilmer Review, governments opened public monopolies and protected industries to competition, which aimed to lower prices and lift productivity. Raising tariffs is the opposite of this reform.

questions.stem: Ending the two-airline policy in 1990 allowed new airlines to enter the domestic market. This is an example of:
options: deregulation
privatisation
nationalisation
a command-and-control instrument
questions.explanation: Deregulation removes government rules that restrict entry or pricing. Privatisation is the sale of a government business to private owners, which is a different reform.

questions.stem: Infrastructure investment, such as upgrading freight rail, is a microeconomic policy mainly because it:
options: lowers the exchange rate and makes exports cheaper overseas
lowers transport costs for businesses and raises productivity
raises the cash rate and reduces the demand for borrowed funds
raises tariff revenue on imported goods arriving at major ports
questions.explanation: Better infrastructure reduces costs and delays for firms, increasing efficiency and productive capacity. It also adds to aggregate demand while it is being built.

questions.stem: A state government replaces stamp duty on property purchases with an annual land tax. Economists support this tax reform mainly because it would:
options: increase the number of homes sold, as the tax rises each time a home changes hands
reduce a barrier to moving home, so housing and labour are used more efficiently
raise the price of land, increasing the wealth of all existing home owners
remove all property taxes, lowering the cost of housing to zero over time
questions.explanation: Stamp duty is a large up-front cost each time a property is bought, which discourages people from moving to a better-suited home or job. A broad land tax raises revenue with smaller effects on such decisions.

questions.stem: Medicare, the PBS and bulk-billing incentives are microeconomic policies in health that aim mainly to:
options: reduce government spending on health care to balance the budget
shorten waiting lists by limiting the number of doctors in training
make health care affordable and reduce inequity in health outcomes
raise the profits of private health insurers and private hospitals
questions.explanation: Subsidised medical services and medicines lower out-of-pocket costs, improving access for lower-income households. These policies increase rather than reduce government health spending.

questions.stem: A government gives first home buyers a cash grant, but the supply of housing is highly inelastic in the short run. The most likely result is:
options: a large increase in new homes built within the first few months
no change in prices, as the grant is paid only to first home buyers
higher house prices, with much of the grant passed on to sellers
lower house prices, as more buyers compete for the same homes
questions.explanation: The grant raises demand, but with supply unable to respond quickly, prices rise instead of quantity. Economists therefore favour policies that also increase housing supply, such as planning reform.

questions.stem: Which policy is aimed at improving housing supply rather than housing demand?
options: Reforming zoning rules to allow more medium-density homes near transport
Increasing cash grants for first home buyers who are purchasing existing homes
Raising Commonwealth Rent Assistance paid to low-income renters
Allowing buyers to withdraw superannuation for a home deposit
questions.explanation: Planning and zoning reform lets more dwellings be built, shifting supply right. Grants, rent assistance and access to super all raise the ability of households to pay, which affects demand.

questions.stem: Regulatory capture occurs when:
options: a regulator sets prices so low that firms leave the regulated industry
a regulator comes to act in the interests of the industry it is supposed to regulate
a government buys a private business and runs it as a public enterprise
a firm gains a monopoly by developing a product that rivals cannot copy
questions.explanation: Close ties, lobbying and the movement of staff between regulator and industry can lead regulators to favour industry over the public. It limits the effectiveness of microeconomic policy.

questions.stem: A limitation of microeconomic reform is that:
options: it can be changed at every meeting of the Reserve Bank's Monetary Policy Board
it affects only aggregate demand and has no effect on the economy's capacity
its benefits take years to appear while its costs, such as job losses, are felt early
it always lowers productivity in the industries that are opened to competition
questions.explanation: Reform often brings early, concentrated costs to particular workers and regions, while gains in efficiency are spread out and delayed. This makes reform politically difficult.

questions.stem: Which is a command-and-control environmental instrument?
options: A subsidy for home battery systems
A ban on single-use plastic bags
A tax on each tonne of emissions
A tradeable emissions permit scheme
questions.explanation: Command-and-control instruments directly regulate behaviour through bans, restrictions and standards. Taxes, permits and subsidies change prices or create markets, so they are market-based.

questions.stem: Minimum energy efficiency ratings that every new refrigerator sold must meet are an example of:
options: a quantity-based market instrument, like a permit scheme
a nudge, because buyers can still choose any refrigerator
an efficiency standard, a command-and-control instrument
a price-based market instrument, like an emissions tax
questions.explanation: A standard that every product must meet is a direct regulation. Buyers cannot purchase a model below the standard, so it is not a nudge.

questions.stem: An emissions permit scheme is classed as:
options: a command-and-control instrument
a technical specification for products
a quantity-based market instrument
a price-based market instrument
questions.explanation: A permit scheme caps the total quantity of emissions and lets the market set the permit price. An emissions tax is price-based: it fixes the price and lets the quantity adjust.

questions.stem: On a negative externality graph, the socially optimal output is 500 units, where MSC = demand. At 500 units, MSC is $40 and MPC is $28. The optimal tax on producers is:
options: $40 per unit
$28 per unit
$68 per unit
$12 per unit
questions.explanation: The optimal tax equals the external cost per unit at the social optimum: MSC - MPC = 40 - 28 = $12. Shifting the private supply curve up by this amount makes the market produce the socially optimal output.

questions.stem: Compared with command-and-control instruments, an advantage of market-based instruments is that:
options: firms that can cut emissions cheaply do the most, lowering the total cost of abatement
the government knows in advance exactly what each firm's costs of abatement will be
they guarantee that every firm reduces its emissions by exactly the same amount
they never raise prices for consumers of emissions-intensive goods and services
questions.explanation: A price on emissions lets each firm choose how much to abate, so cuts happen where they are cheapest. Uniform rules ignore differences in costs and so cost more for the same result.

questions.stem: When might a command-and-control instrument be preferred to a market-based instrument?
options: When the government wants to raise revenue from polluting firms
When the aim is to cut emissions at the lowest possible total cost
When a pollutant is so harmful that any amount must be prevented
When firms' costs of reducing pollution differ widely from one to another
questions.explanation: For highly toxic substances an outright ban gives certainty that harm is eliminated. Where abatement costs differ, the case for market-based instruments is strongest.

questions.stem: Under the Climate Change Act 2022, Australia's legislated targets are to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by:
options: 60% below 2000 levels by 2030, and to reach net zero by 2040
43% below 2005 levels by 2030, and to reach net zero by 2050
43% below 1990 levels by 2030, and to reach net zero by 2070
26% below 2005 levels by 2030, and to reach net zero by 2060
questions.explanation: The Act legislates a 2030 target of 43% below 2005 levels and net zero by 2050. Earlier commitments under the Paris Agreement were a 26-28% cut by 2030.

questions.stem: Australia's emissions targets are communicated internationally under the Paris Agreement of 2015. Their influence on domestic policy is shown by:
options: policies such as the Safeguard Mechanism, which lowers emissions limits for large facilities
the abolition of all state government renewable energy targets and programs
a ban on the export of coal and gas to all other countries from 2030 onwards
the setting of the cash rate by the Reserve Bank to meet the emissions target
questions.explanation: The reformed Safeguard Mechanism requires facilities emitting over 100,000 tonnes of CO2-e a year to keep below baselines that decline each year, to help meet national targets. Coal and gas exports have not been banned.

questions.stem: The Safeguard Mechanism sets declining emissions limits (baselines) for Australia's largest industrial emitters. Facilities that beat their baseline can earn credits to sell to others. This makes it:
options: a ban, a command-and-control instrument with no trading allowed
a nudge, because facilities can ignore their baselines freely
a baseline-and-credit scheme, a quantity-based market instrument
a carbon tax, a price-based market instrument with a fixed price
questions.explanation: Limiting emissions relative to baselines and allowing trade in credits for surplus reductions creates a market in emissions within a cap on each facility. It does not set a fixed tax price.

questions.stem: Carbon leakage occurs when:
options: greenhouse gases escape from storage sites after being captured underground
a carbon tax raises more revenue than the government expected to collect
consumers switch from petrol cars to electric vehicles much faster than forecast
emissions-intensive production moves to countries with weaker climate policies
questions.explanation: If firms relocate to countries without carbon pricing, domestic emissions fall but global emissions may not, and local jobs are lost. Concern about leakage shapes protections for trade-exposed industries.

questions.stem: A limitation of Australia acting alone to cut emissions is the global free rider problem. This means that:
options: Australia receives the full benefit of its emission cuts, so other countries need not act
other countries gain from Australia's cuts without bearing their cost, weakening their incentive to act
Australian households receive cheap renewable electricity without paying any network charges
firms in Australia can use public roads and ports without paying for the cost of their upkeep
questions.explanation: A stable climate is a global public good, so every country benefits from cuts made anywhere. Each country is tempted to let others bear the cost, which is why international agreements matter.

questions.stem: Which is a policy lag limiting environmental policy?
options: Bans on products can be ignored by all firms without penalty
International agreements are binding only on poor countries
New low-emission power plants take years to plan and build
Emission taxes take effect the moment they are announced
questions.explanation: Changing the capital stock, such as power stations and vehicle fleets, takes many years, so policies work slowly. Bans are enforceable, and the Paris Agreement applies to all parties.

questions.stem: The policy mix refers to:
options: the share of the government budget spent on health, education and welfare in a year
the balance between exports and imports in Australia's current account each quarter
the combination of macroeconomic and microeconomic policies used to achieve economic objectives
the choice between raising taxes and cutting spending when the budget is in deficit
questions.explanation: Governments combine fiscal, monetary, microeconomic, labour market and environmental policies, because no single policy can achieve every objective. Coordination avoids policies working against one another.

questions.stem: Why is a coordinated policy mix needed to achieve both short-term and long-term objectives?
options: Fiscal policy alone can achieve every objective, so other policies are not required
Microeconomic policies work faster than monetary policy in a sudden downturn
Demand management stabilises the cycle, while supply-side policies lift long-run capacity
Monetary policy lifts long-run capacity, while microeconomic policy stabilises the cycle
questions.explanation: Fiscal and monetary policy manage aggregate demand in the short term, while microeconomic, labour market and environmental policies raise productivity and sustainability over time. The roles are complementary.

questions.stem: Inflation is above the RBA's target while the government runs a large expansionary budget. What problem does this policy mix create?
options: Monetary and fiscal policy both reduce demand, so the economy will fall into a deep recession
Fiscal policy restrains demand while monetary policy adds to it, so inflation will rise further
Both policies are neutral, so neither will affect inflation or employment in the short term
Fiscal policy adds to demand while monetary policy restrains it, so interest rates may need to rise further
questions.explanation: When the budget stimulates demand while the RBA is trying to lower inflation, the two pull in opposite directions. The RBA may then need a higher cash rate to achieve the same result, which shows the value of coordination.

questions.stem: During the COVID-19 downturn of 2020, the government expanded spending while the RBA cut the cash rate and used unconventional measures. This mix is best described as:
options: coordinated expansionary policy to respond to a severe economic shock
coordinated contractionary policy to bring inflation back to target
conflicting policy, as fiscal and monetary policy pulled in opposite directions
microeconomic reform to raise productivity over the long term
questions.explanation: Both arms of macroeconomic policy were set to support demand and employment during the shock. Programs such as JobKeeper and record-low interest rates worked in the same direction.

questions.stem: A government wants to reduce emissions while protecting low-income households from higher energy prices. Which policy package best balances these objectives?
options: Abolition of energy efficiency standards to keep appliance prices low for buyers
An emissions price, with part of the revenue returned to low-income households
A subsidy for coal-fired electricity, paid for by higher income tax on low incomes
A ban on all household electricity use during peak periods with no compensation
questions.explanation: Pricing emissions encourages abatement, while recycling revenue to low-income households addresses equity. The other options either raise emissions or impose costs without addressing fairness.

questions.stem: Evaluate this proposal: to cut inflation, the government raises the GST rate. Which is the strongest criticism?
options: It would have no effect on aggregate demand, as consumption taxes do not change prices
It would lower government revenue and push the budget into a larger deficit immediately
It would raise the price level directly in the short term and fall hardest on lower-income households
It would raise the incomes of lower-income households and so add to demand-pull inflation
questions.explanation: A GST rise lifts measured prices at once, even if it later restrains demand, and consumption taxes are regressive. Policy evaluation weighs effects on all objectives, including equity.

questions.stem: Which combination best addresses both housing affordability and long-term productivity?
options: A higher cash rate combined with larger first home buyer grants
Planning reform and infrastructure that increase housing supply near jobs
Higher grants for buyers and tighter limits on new building approvals
Rent controls set well below market rents across all major cities
questions.explanation: More homes near jobs and transport improve affordability and let workers live closer to where they are most productive. Grants and rent controls set below market do not add to supply.

questions.stem: Quality of life is a broad objective. Which indicator would best show progress towards it beyond economic growth alone?
options: A larger budget surplus achieved by cutting spending on public services
Faster growth in total output achieved by longer average working hours
Improvements in health, education, environmental quality and leisure
A rise in nominal GDP caused mainly by a higher general price level
questions.explanation: Quality of life includes material and non-material wellbeing such as health, education, the environment and time for leisure. Higher nominal GDP or longer hours may not improve wellbeing.

questions.stem: Which instrument is a price-based market instrument?
options: A fuel efficiency standard for cars
A tax on each tonne of emissions
A cap on total emissions with permits
A ban on burning coal for power
questions.explanation: A tax sets the price of emitting and leaves firms to choose how much to emit. A cap-and-trade scheme fixes the quantity, while bans and standards are command-and-control.
